title: Community Tour Guide
goal: Your kid becomes the tour guide for a place they know: your street, a favourite park, the town centre. They dig up stories about each stop, plan a route, and lead a real walking tour for family or friends. Kids are usually amazed by what they find out about a place they walk past every day.
create: A route with 3 to 6 stops in a place they know
Notes and a short script with the facts and stories for each stop
A live walking tour, led by them, for family or friends
need: A local place to explore: your street, a park, the town centre, a trail, or even your garden
A notebook for notes and the script, and comfortable shoes
An audience: family, friends, grandparents or neighbours

howTo.intro: No teaching experience needed. You're the behind-the-scenes producer, the most enthusiastic guest on tour day, and in charge of safety on the walk.

plan.what: The house tour, then choose the place and the stops (Step 1). About 20 minutes.
Walk the route, dig up the stories, write the script (Steps 2 and 3).
One practice walk, then the real tour (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: Your kid is shy about speaking
troubleshoot.a: Start with a tour for just you, then add one more person. Cue cards with one line per stop help a lot.
Tours can be about nature, food or their own stories: the climbing tree, the bakery, where they learned to ride a bike.

skills.name: Public speaking
skills.text: speaking clearly and confidently to a live audience

skills.name: Research
skills.text: finding real facts and stories about a place

skills.name: Storytelling
skills.text: turning facts into something people want to listen to

skills.name: Planning
skills.text: putting stops in an order that flows from start to finish

steps.title: Give a house tour
steps.why: A silly practice tour of your home, then the real place and its stops.
steps.kid: Your kid gives you a 3-minute tour of your own home, as if you were a visitor who's never been inside. At each room they point at something, tell you one thing about it, and ask you a question. Then they pick the real place for the tour, walk it with fresh eyes, and choose the stops a first-time visitor would find interesting.
steps.you: Play the clueless visitor for the house tour and ask silly questions. Then help them think of places and walk the area together. Ask what they'd show a friend from another town, and let them choose.
ask: What would a visitor never notice here unless you pointed it out?
If a friend visited from another town, where would you take them first?
steps.tip: Walking a place on purpose changes how kids see it. They'll spot plaques, old signs and dates they've walked past a hundred times.

levels.explore: Give the house tour with one thing to say per room, then choose 3 or 4 stops.
levels.develop: Use point, tell, ask in every room, then walk the area and choose 5 or 6 stops.
levels.extend: Sketch a rough map of the real place as you walk, choose 6 or more stops, and note what to research at each.

steps.title: Dig up the stories
steps.why: Your kid finds the facts and stories that make each stop worth stopping for.
steps.kid: For each stop, your kid looks for 2 or 3 things the audience won't already know: when it was built, who used to live or work there, something about the plants or animals, or a story that happened there. They look closely, read signs and plaques, look things up, and ask people who know the area. They note where each fact came from.
steps.you: Help them get to sources: the library, a local history website, an old photo, or a long-time neighbour. Don't do the research for them. If a fact sounds too good to be true, ask how they could check it.
ask: What could you tell someone about this place that would surprise them?
Who would know more about this? Could we ask them?
steps.tip: Neighbours and local shop owners are the best sources. A story from someone who was there beats anything in a book, and kids love collecting them.

levels.explore: Find 1 or 2 interesting facts about each stop.
levels.develop: Find 2 or 3 facts per stop from at least two sources, and mark the most surprising ones.
levels.extend: Research history, nature or culture at each stop, and interview a local person for an insider story.

steps.title: Plan the route and the script
steps.why: Your kid puts the stops in order and writes what they'll say.
steps.kid: Your kid puts the stops in an order that makes sense to walk and draws a simple map. Then they write what they'll say: a welcome, point, tell and ask for each stop, what to say while walking, and a closing that thanks everyone. Bullet points are fine.
steps.you: Walk the route together and time it. Then read or listen to the script and help with clarity, not content: is anything confusing? Is there a part that drags? Where's the best story? Let them decide what to change.
ask: Should you start with your best stop, or save it for the end?
How will you grab everyone's attention at the very first stop?
steps.tip: Aim for 15 to 30 minutes. Shorter and punchier beats long and complete, especially for a first tour.

levels.explore: Put the stops in order, draw a simple route, and write 2 or 3 sentences per stop with a welcome and goodbye.
levels.develop: Time the walk, adjust the order, and write a full script with an introduction, notes for each stop, transitions and a closing.
levels.extend: Make a detailed map with times and distances, and add a strong opening story, connections between stops, and a question for the audience at each stop.

steps.title: Practise on location
steps.why: Your kid rehearses the whole tour, out loud, on the real route.
steps.kid: Your kid walks the route and gives the tour out loud at each stop, as if the audience were there. They practise speaking loud enough for a group, looking up from their notes, and pointing at what they're talking about. They time it, then fix anything that feels too long, too short or awkward.
steps.you: Be the practice audience. Afterward, give feedback on volume, pace and eye contact: 'Could I hear you? Did you look at me or at your notes?' Start with something they did well.
ask: Did you look at your audience, or mostly at your notes?
Which part do you feel most confident about?
steps.tip: Practising on location makes the biggest difference. Standing at the real spot is when the words start to come naturally.

levels.explore: Walk the route and practise saying the key facts at each stop.
levels.develop: Do one full practice tour, time it, and revise 1 or 2 parts based on how it went.
levels.extend: Do 2 full practice runs: revise after the first, then do the second without looking at your script.

steps.title: Lead the tour and look back
steps.why: The real tour, with a real audience, and a look back at how it went.
steps.kid: Your kid welcomes the group, leads them from stop to stop and gives the tour. At each stop, they share their facts and stories, and get the audience involved: a question, something to look for, a surprising fact. They close by thanking everyone. Afterward, they ask the audience what they liked most and think about what they'd change next time.
steps.you: Be an engaged, enthusiastic guest. Ask a question or two, take photos, and celebrate the effort no matter how it goes. Afterward, give specific praise: 'The story about the old tree was my favourite part.' Then ask what they're most proud of.
ask: Did you notice the audience react to anything you said?
If you gave the tour again tomorrow, what would you change?
steps.tip: If they forget something, nobody knows. Remind them before the tour: keep going, and the audience will never notice.

levels.explore: Lead the group through your stops, sharing at least one fact at each, and tell someone one thing that went well.
levels.develop: Give the full tour, ask the audience at least one question, and write a short reflection with their feedback.
levels.extend: Give a polished tour with audience interaction and a strong closing, then write about what you learned about speaking to a group.

conclusion.headline: Your kid just researched, planned and led a real walking tour.
conclusion.text: They picked a place, dug up its stories, planned a route and led a real group through it. Speaking, local history and map skills, with an audience walking right behind them.
conclusion.celebrate: Point out what took courage: they stood in front of people, shared what they'd found and led the whole thing from start to finish. Lots of adults would find that hard.
extensions: Give a tour of a completely different place: a market, a museum or a new neighbourhood
Record the tour as a video for family who couldn't come
Make a printed tour brochure someone could follow on their own
Give the same tour to a new audience and compare how it went
Plan a themed tour: history, nature, food or buildings

cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

photo.alt: Two kids on scooters riding toward a covered bridge, next to a tall clock tower
photo.caption: Your town already has the stops. Your kid just has to find the stories.

lesson.text: A good tour stop does three things: point at something people can see, tell one thing they didn't know, and ask them a question. Teach it at the first stop and your kid will use it at every one.
lesson.before: This is the library. It's old. Okay, next stop.

model.line: Look up above the door. See the date carved in the stone?
That's the year it was built, when this street was still a dirt road.
Who can guess what this building was used for before it was a library?
Follow me to the bridge. Watch for the plaque on the left.

lesson.modelNote: Same stop, but now people are looking, thinking and following. When a stop is just a name and a fact, ask: what can they see, and what will you ask them?

makeItReal: Offer the tour to someone who's actually new: visiting grandparents, a new neighbour, a friend's family who just moved. A guest who really doesn't know the place makes every fact land.
